title: Tantalus and his torment
subtitle: So close, never enough
subject: mythologie
description: Tantalus serves his own son to the gods. His sentence: water and fruit forever out of reach. A myth of frustration that even named a chemical element.

hero.hook: The water comes up to his chin. The fruit hangs above his head. And never a sip, never a bite.

blocks.text: **Tantalus** is excess and its punishment in one figure. Invited to eat at the table of the gods, this favored king dared to test them. His sentence was refined: to see what he wants right in front of him, and never be able to take it.
The myth has passed into language, into psychology and even into chemistry. To suffer the torment of Tantalus is still the name we give to absolute frustration.

sections.title: A king too close to the gods

blocks.text: Tantalus was king of Lydia, in Asia Minor. Son of **Zeus** and a nymph, he was sometimes allowed to share the nectar and ambrosia of Olympus. That closeness made him arrogant. First he stole the food of the gods and handed it out to other mortals.

Then came the horror. To test whether the gods really see everything, he invited the whole pantheon to a banquet. He killed his own son, **Pelops**, cut him up and served him as the main dish. The gods drew back. Only **Demeter**, goddess of the harvest, distracted by grief for her daughter [[Persephone]], bit into a piece of the shoulder.
Zeus brought Pelops back to life. The eaten shoulder was replaced by a piece of [[ivory]]. The line of Tantalus, the **House of Atreus**, stayed cursed: Agamemnon and Orestes would inherit it.

sections.title: The water that drains, the fruit that lifts away

blocks.text: In [[Tartarus]], the deep prison beneath the world, the sentence turned the crime inside out. He had insulted the sacred banquet, so he would never eat again. Sunk up to his chin in a lake, he was dying of thirst.

blocks.caption: Tantalus, surrounded by water and fruit he cannot reach

blocks.text: The moment he bent his head, the water sank into the ground. Above him, branches hung heavy with figs, pears and pomegranates. The moment he reached out, a wind pushed them away. What tortures him is not absence: it is the false promise of nearness.
One version adds a third threat: a huge rock hanging over his head, ready to fall. No rest, even setting hunger aside.

sections.title: From myth to the periodic table

blocks.text: In **1802**, the Swedish chemist **Anders Ekeberg** found a new metal. He named it **tantalum** (atomic number **73**): plunged into acid, it absorbs almost nothing. Just like the thirsty king standing in a lake.

blocks.caption: Tantalum, element 73, named after the myth

blocks.text: Today the [[chemical element tantalum (Ta, 73)]] is a strategic material: capacitors in smartphones, implants that resist corrosion. In English, *to tantalize* means to stir up desire while holding the prize just out of reach. The verb comes straight from the name of the king.
[[The "tantalizing punishment" as archetype]] names any situation where the goal seems within reach, then slips away at the last moment.
In psychology, Tantalus stands for a desire that never burns out: the closer the object, the sharper the failure. In politics, the image fits promises that move away as soon as you get near them.
His crime was not only a murder. It was an attempt to deceive the gods. In return, his own senses deceive him for eternity: he sees the water, he sees the fruit, and he holds nothing.

**Tantalus**, king of Lydia, served his son **Pelops** to the gods. Sentenced to Tartarus, he has water and fruit before his eyes and can never reach them. His name lives on in our language and in element **73**.
